summary.title: The Engineer/Manager Pendulum
summary.one_liner: Engineers can grow by moving back and forth between hands-on engineering and management over time, rather than picking one lane, and management is a change of profession rather than a promotion.
keywords: serial vs simultaneous management and coding
when to stop managing and return to coding
leaving management to go back to hands-on work
takeaways: Moving between engineering and management in cycles can be a deliberate, valid career path rather than a one-way track.
Management is a change of profession and a lateral move onto a parallel track, so new managers are often bad at it for a long time.
You can only meaningfully improve at one of engineering or management at a time; hybrid manager-plus-tech-lead roles are unstable.
The best tech leads usually have spent time in management, since they need people-management tools even when focused on the task.
Managers should stop managing when it no longer makes them and their team happy, rather than staying for status.
summary.summary: Charity Majors argues against the idea that only managers get career progression and that engineers must pick a lane. She describes a pendulum pattern of moving between hands-on engineering and management, serially rather than simultaneously, and says the best frontline managers stay within 2-3 years of hands-on work. The post contrasts the focused-attention demands of coding with the interruption-heavy nature of management, and frames management as a change of profession rather than a promotion. It is an opinion essay drawing on personal experience and tweets by Sarah Mei, with no code or formal tutorial steps.
